title: Contemporary Mission, Inc. v. Famous Music Corporation
lead: A record company’s sale of its division interrupted two music agreements, and the resulting appeal separated continuing performance duties from uncertain projections of artistic success.

actors.name: Contemporary Mission
actors.role: Nonprofit corporation of priests producing music

actors.name: Famous Music
actors.role: Contracting record company selling its division

actors.name: ABC
actors.role: Purchaser that did not continue performance

actors.name: Father John O’Reilly and Tony Martell

proceedings: Jury awarded under Virgin, Crunch, an unallocated category, and an oral reimbursement agreement.
Second Circuit affirmed except the lost-royalty evidentiary ruling and remanded for Rule 403 balancing.
limits: The remand did not unconditionally order admission, a new trial, or added royalties. Oral reimbursement and dismissed parent-company claims were not appealed. Possible ABC liability and Famous indemnification remained reserved.

review.basis: Individually written and compared with the canonical full brief; no new independent opinion audit claimed.

sections.title: Two agreements place recordings with Famous
paragraphs: Contemporary Mission was a nonprofit corporation of Roman Catholic priests who wrote and produced music. It owned Father John O’Reilly’s rock opera Virgin. Famous Music president Tony Martell, experienced with Tommy and Jesus Christ Superstar, hoped for similar success. Their August 16, 1972 agreement exchanged the master and exclusive manufacturing and sales rights for royalties, a personal promotional overseer, at least $50,000 first-year promotion, and four singles in two years. Assignment in specified transactions required delivery of an undertaking binding the assignee to Famous’s obligations.

A May 8, 1973 Crunch agreement covered other recordings under a new label, with exclusive domestic distribution, Contemporary delivery requirements, and Famous’s reasonable promotional efforts. Material default required a written specification and thirty days without cure. It restricted Contemporary’s assignments but not Famous’s, while paragraph 12 denied power to create obligations in the other party’s name.

sections.title: The division sale interrupts the relationship
sections.cue: The jury distinguishes pre-sale promotion from later nonperformance
paragraphs: Results had disappointed initial hopes, but relations stayed amicable until Famous sold its record division to ABC July 31, 1974. Martell directed O’Reilly to ABC; an ABC lawyer said it would have no relationship with Contemporary. Records left retail outlets for ABC. Contemporary’s August notices objected to the transaction and removal, then it sued.

At trial before Judge Richard Owen, the jury found inadequate Virgin promotion and damage from its assignment, plus ABC’s refusal to perform Crunch and resulting damage. It expressly found Famous had used required reasonable Crunch efforts before assignment. Awards were $68,773 under Virgin, $104,751 under Crunch, $21,000 unallocated, and $16,500 on an oral reimbursement agreement. The last issue and dismissals of Gulf + Western and Paramount were not appealed.

Famous did not challenge the instruction that assigning Virgin without ABC’s written undertaking breached that clause. It contested the independent promotion finding. Contemporary cross-appealed exclusion of projected royalty evidence.

sections.title: Famous remains responsible for both promises
sections.cue: The majority finds enough promotion evidence and notice
paragraphs: Judge Meskill, joined by Judge Mansfield, held the exclusive Virgin grant also implied reasonable national promotion under Wood v. Lucy. Spending and an overseer did not exhaust that duty. Ending one single’s promotion prematurely, local test marketing another, and staff reductions supported the close jury determination. Spending evidence, though uncontradicted, was imprecise and self-serving. An amendment permitting cessation when promotion lost effectiveness and profitability required a good-faith determination, not arbitrary discretion; none was shown. The overseer requirement had been met, but other duties remained. An unchallenged oral-proof issue involving a lost business record was reserved.

For Crunch, transfer of rights and delegation of duties were distinct. Assuming without deciding that Martell-linked promotion was delegable, delegation did not discharge Famous. Contemporary showed nobody performed after the sale; it need not prove ABC’s independently actionable repudiation or disprove an unpleaded performance defense. Admission of the ABC lawyer’s statement therefore was not essential.

The notices’ incorrect focus on paragraph 12 did not defeat them. Read with the telegram and conversation, their reference to removal sufficiently identified the interruption and called on Famous to ensure performance. The cure provision was not a pleading trap, and Famous’s disposal of its division left it unable to cure. Contemporary’s claim that assignment was void did not estop recovery on Famous’s own outstanding duty. Potential claims against ABC or indemnity between the companies were reserved.

sections.title: Existing sales establish some lost royalties
sections.cue: An imagined chain of later ventures remains too uncertain
paragraphs: Contemporary sought statistics and expert conversion of chart success into additional royalties for Virgin’s Fear No Evil. New York distinguished certainty of loss from precision of amount. Artistic taste made success uncertain, but this recording already had a market and fixed price. Even after promotion and inventory withdrawal, momentum produced 10,000 more sales and a rise from about number eighty to sixty-one on Billboard’s Hot Soul Singles chart. Some further sales with continued availability and promotion were sufficiently certain.
The proposed domino effects—album sales, concerts, and theatrical tours arising from a hit—depended too much on taste to establish that those losses existed. Their exclusion stood.

A study of 324 songs reaching number sixty-one in 1974 showed 76% reached the top forty, 65% thirty, 51% twenty, 34% ten, 21% five, and 10% number one. An expert proposed translating positions into sales and royalties. Missing information about speed of ascent, performer reputation, and promotion affected weight rather than basic relevance, with contrary proof available.

sections.title: Rule 403 still may exclude relevant projections
sections.cue: The partial dissent would end the inquiry and reverse other awards
paragraphs: Relevance did not decide admissibility. Federal Rule of Evidence 403 permitted exclusion where unfair prejudice, confusion, or misleading force substantially outweighed probative value. Bare statistics might appear stronger than warranted without omitted factors. The district court relied on Freund’s substantive certainty rule without that balance; the majority remanded for the judge to perform it and determine whether Contemporary should receive a new damages trial.

Judge Van Graafeiland agreed on Virgin’s liability and award but would reverse Crunch and the unallocated award. He read the notices as attacking a permissible sale rather than specifying performance default and allowing cure; he also noted no written notice to ABC, which acquired notice rights. He opposed evidentiary remand, believing the judge already examined the foundation and reasonably excluded misleading projections given omitted reputation, quality, promotion, and chart-speed evidence.

On May 18, 1977, the Second Circuit affirmed in all respects except the lost-royalties ruling, remanding for Rule 403 determination. It neither awarded added royalties nor required unconditional admission or a new trial.

sources.pinpoint: 557 F.2d at 928–930 & majority n.17, dissent n.1
